result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the Athenian Acropolis, listing statues and paintings, a strange sacrificial ritual, and the great gold and ivory Athene in the Parthenon. He ends with Phidias' Apollo and a remark on locusts.

scenes.title: Statues and votives on Acropolis
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues and myth groups, including Athene and Marsyas, Theseus and the Minotaur, Phrixus, and Hercules, and describes the Zeus Guardian ox sacrifice.

scenes.title: The Parthenon and its Athene
scenes.summary: He describes the Parthenon gables and the ivory and gold statue of Athene, with a digression on griffins and Arimaspians, and the birth of Pandora on the base.

scenes.title: Adrian, Iphicrates, Apollo and locusts
scenes.summary: He notes statues of Adrian and Iphicrates and Phidias' Apollo Averter of Locusts, adding his own experience of locusts' destruction.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of the god at Orchomenus, conjectured as the recipient of Phrixus' sacrifice.

notable_quotes.reason: Describes the odd Athenian ritual of putting the axe on trial.
Records the birth of Pandora and Hesiod's view that no women existed before her.

analysis.text: Pausanias catalogues art and cult, showing Athenian piety and his interest in myth, ritual and rival traditions.
The Parthenon's chryselephantine Athene, with Hadrian's statue nearby, shows how classical monuments were still visited in the Roman era.

legacy.text: Pausanias' description of Phidias' Athene Parthenos is a key source for reconstructing the lost statue.

fun_facts.text: The ritual with the axe on trial refers to the Athenian Bouphonia, an ox-sacrifice festival.

language_notes.text: Athene invented the flute but threw it away because playing distorted her face; the satyr Marsyas picked it up and was later punished.
Phrixus fled with his sister Helle on a golden-fleeced ram; he reached Colchis and sacrificed the ram, whose fleece the Argonauts later sought.
Laphystius was a title of Zeus at Orchomenus in Boeotia, linked to the Phrixus story and to a tradition of sacrificing the ram.
The infant Hercules strangled the two snakes sent by Hera to kill him in his cradle.
"Mutilated Hermæ" are square pillar-statues of Hermes, with head and phallus; "worker" refers to Athene Ergane, patron of crafts.
Pausanias often declines to give explanations of rites, here saying he records the customs without the reasons offered.
This is the Bouphonia, the ox-murder ritual: the axe was tried in court and thrown into the sea, so no one bore guilt.
Parthenon means the temple of the maiden (parthenos), a title of Athene; "pourtrayed" is an old spelling of portrayed, and gables are the triangular pediments.
Aristæus of Proconnesus wrote an early poem about northern peoples, the Arimaspians and Issedones, and is Pausanias' source for the griffin story.
A cubit is about the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches, so the Victory is about six feet tall.
Erichthonius was an early Athenian hero-king born from the earth and raised by Athene, often shown as a snake; Pausanias is unsure the dragon is him.
Pandora is the first woman in Hesiod's Works and Days and Theogony, made by the gods and bringing evils to men.
Adrian is this translation's spelling of the Emperor Hadrian.
"Brazen" means made of bronze; "Averter" translates the title of a god who turns away a pest.

context_notes.text: Theseus, Athenian hero, killed the Minotaur, a half-bull monster kept in the Cretan Labyrinth.
The Areopagus was Athens' ancient council, which met on the hill of Ares and judged homicide cases.
Cleœtas was a sculptor; the silver nails show the taste for detail in later bronze work.
Procne killed her son Itys to punish her husband Tereus, who had wronged her sister Philomela.
This recalls the contest of Athene and Poseidon for Athens: she offered the olive, he a salt spring.
The Sphinx is a winged monster with a woman's head and a lion's body, best known from the Theban story of Oedipus.
Iphicrates was an Athenian general of the early fourth century BC, known for reforming the use of light-armed troops.
Phidias was the famous fifth-century Athenian sculptor who also made the great gold and ivory Athene inside the Parthenon.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias lightly defends the Minotaur myth by pointing to monstrous births in his own day, a sober, skeptical aside.
The Athenians are portrayed as exceptionally pious, a theme Pausanias uses to justify their many sacred monuments.
Earth is shown as a woman begging Zeus for rain, making a natural need a human plea.
The axe is tried as if guilty while everyone knows the priest struck, a ritual pretense of innocence.
Pausanias abruptly cuts off his digression, showing the guidebook's businesslike voice and his awareness of staying on the tour.
The Athenians are sure of the miracle yet cannot explain it, and Pausanias gently exposes the gap in their claim.
Pausanias presents himself as a careful eyewitness, offering natural causes for the locusts' destruction beside the god's supposed intervention.
